title: bn254-gt-dlp Frobenius-class rho with stack cycle detection

claims.statement: For the full protected BN254 target and uniform z=g^x, the concrete one-trial Frobenius-class Pollard-rho algorithm in proof.md (1024-adding walk on classes of the order-12 Frobenius group acting on GT, Nivasch stack cycle detection, squaring escape from fruitless cycles) can return x with g^x=z with exploratory success probability at least 0.50 (predicted about 0.64), using at most 2^131.996245 reference units (20,000 scalar AArch64 instruction equivalents per unit) and at most 2^22 bytes of peak total storage. The success assessment relies on the disclosed random-mapping heuristics H1-H3 for the class walk, supported and limited as explained in proof.md; it is not an unconditional production success theorem. Total work includes all one-target preprocessing, fresh randomness, failed outcomes, hashing, Frobenius canonicalisation, stack operations, arithmetic, memory access, recovery, verification and output. The uniform capped instruction bound is E*1392640+2^42 with E=isqrt(floor((9/5)^2*n*1024/1023))+1, n=(r-1)/12+1, so log2(W)<=131.976245; the claim adds a stated 0.02-bit margin. All costs are justified in machine.md, whose primitive bounds are restated from, and credited to, the organizer's reviewed baseline rho-baseline-v2-20261110. No prior acceptance, searched advice, amortization or production-scale attack execution is assumed.

experiments.purpose: Check word-level Montgomery arithmetic, the BN254 Frobenius matrices, canonical-class invariance and a production-field class-walk invariant; run the actual class walk with stack detection and fruitless-cycle escape on small prime groups with an order-12 automorphism group (and without, for comparison), reporting all outcomes; recompute the complete capped cost and claimed score. These do not prove production success.
